newsitem.title: NEPAL: Nepal and India renew trade treaty for five years.
newsitem.headline: Nepal and India renew trade treaty for five years.

text.p: India offered improved terms of trade to Nepal on Tuesday after the two countries renewed a five-year trade treaty, officials said.
"It is a landmark departure from the past practices which will help industries by attracting foreign investment," Mohan Dev Pant, Nepal's Commerce Secretary, said.
The treaty would allow most Nepali products into the Indian market duty free on a non-reciprocal basis, officials said.
Only alcohol, cigarettes and cosmetic exports to India would attract tariffs, they said.
The provisions replace arrangements in the 1991 trade treaty, which offered zero tariffs on only those Nepali items with at least 50 percent Nepali or Indian material content.
"The treaty has been renewed for another five years with provisions for auto renewal unless either country has any amendments or objections," an official statement said.
Tejendra Khanna, the highest ranking civil servant in India's commerce ministry, and Pant signed the treaty in Kathmandu on Tuesday.
"India has a role in taking the initiative to liberalise trade in the region," Khanna told a news conference after the treaty signing.
Twenty-nine percent of Nepal's total trade is with India.
The Himalayan kingdom's trade deficit with India widened to $380.6 million in the 1994/95 financial year, which ended in mid-July 1995, up from $306.6 million the previous year.
Trade has been a major irritant in India's relationship with Nepal, one of the world's 10 poorest countries. In 1989, New Delhi refused to renew trade and transit treaties.
Only one entry point was allowed to landlocked Nepal along the 1,000 km (625 mile) border with India.
Both treaties were renewed in 1991 after multi-party parliamentary democracy was restored in Nepal six years ago. The transit treaty will expire in 1998.
